title: I follow curiosity.
Then I build.
lede: I started in Civil Engineering, moved into Data, and found my way into AI.
Along the way, I learned that the work I enjoy most usually starts with a question: can this be understood better, made simpler, or built differently?
So I explore it. Then I try to build it.

title: I did not start
in tech.
body: Civil Engineering was the path I started with. It made sense at the time. It connected with my family's direction, and mathematics had always been one of my strengths.

I worked across construction, BIM, and geotechnical engineering. Each role showed me a different side of engineering, from coordinating work on site to translating drawings into 3D models and working with technical calculations.
Then I started working with much larger datasets.

title: The questions
changed.
body: At G&P, some of my work involved millions of time-series equipment readings.
I needed to visualize them, identify abnormal readings, understand patterns, and sometimes look at how those readings might develop over time.
The repetitive parts made me curious.
questions: Could I process this with Python?
Could I make this Excel workflow easier with VBA?
after: Those questions gradually became more interesting to me than the engineering problem itself.
That was my way into Data.

title: From using data
to building around it.
body: Moving into a Data Analyst role gave me the opportunity to make Data my actual work.
I started with reporting and Power BI, working with dashboards, transforming data, and preparing information so it could be used properly for analysis.
But I kept becoming interested in what happened before the dashboard.
questions: Where did the data come from?
How do we move it reliably?
What happens when the volume grows?
What should happen when something fails?
after: That curiosity pulled me further into Data Engineering.

Today, my work sits across Data Engineering and AI. I work on migration, automation, data quality, and AI-assisted systems, including agentic workflows that turn data into recommendations and usable application outputs.

title: Data led me
to AI.
body: I have been fascinated by the idea of intelligent technology for a long time. What changed as I worked more deeply with Data was that AI stopped feeling like an abstract idea.
It became something I could actually build with.

Machine Learning gave me another way to understand patterns in data. Generative AI opened different ways for people to interact with information. Agentic workflows introduced new questions about how AI could reason over data, recommend actions, and work alongside existing systems.
I am still exploring those questions.
That is part of what keeps the field interesting to me.

title: Most of my projects start
with something bothering me.

origins.text: Writing repetitive ETL logic made me wonder whether working with messy data could be more direct.

origins.lead: Sometimes it comes from everyday life.
origins.text: Organizing volleyball sessions through messages and individual coordination felt unnecessarily difficult.
I like how Formula 1 uses data to understand performance, so I started experimenting with what a 3D racing experience built around real data could look like.

after: I do not always know whether an idea will work when I start.
For me, building is how I find out.

title: Progress usually
comes from iteration.
body: I like understanding a problem by working through it.
Start with what is available. Build something tangible. Test it. Find what does not work. Change it. Repeat.
The first version rarely needs to be perfect. It needs to teach me enough to make the next version better.

title: Learning is better
when I can pass it on.
body: My long-term goal is not only to work in Data and AI, but to understand the field deeply enough to make it useful to other people.
That has gradually taken me from learning and building to sharing and teaching.

I have conducted internal technical sessions for colleagues, spoken to students about what they can explore with Google's Data and AI technologies, and delivered structured Cloud and AI training for public-sector professionals.
Teaching has also changed how I learn.
If I cannot explain something clearly, I probably need to understand it better.

title: Away from the screen.
body: When I am not working or building something, there is a good chance I am running, playing volleyball, following Formula 1, or finding another interest that eventually turns into a project.
Apparently, leaving hobbies as hobbies is something I am still working on.
